context: Wartime plan for universal schooling (the Butler Act).
did: Made secondary education free for all, raised the leaving age to 15 (from 1947) and set up the Ministry of Education with a duty on local education authorities to provide schools.
effects: Created the state school system that still exists; the selective 11-plus 'tripartite' structure it enabled was largely replaced by comprehensives from 1965.

did: Created a single contributory scheme paying unemployment, sickness, maternity, widows' and retirement benefits in return for flat-rate contributions.
effects: Foundation of today's contributory benefits and the state pension; National Insurance became a de facto second income tax over time.

context: Bevan's plan to replace a patchwork of voluntary, municipal and insurance-based care.
did: Nationalised hospitals and created a comprehensive health service free at the point of use from 5 July 1948.
effects: The founding NHS statute, since consolidated into the NHS Act 2006. Health is now the largest single area of departmental spending.

context: Post-war housing shortage and slum clearance.
did: Let the government designate new towns built by development corporations with powers to buy land at existing-use value.
effects: 32 new towns, among them Stevenage, Milton Keynes and Harlow. Its land-value capture model is the precedent cited for today's new towns programme.

context: Unplanned inter-war sprawl and post-war reconstruction.
did: Nationalised the right to develop land: from 1948 almost all development needed planning permission from the local planning authority.
effects: The discretionary planning system that is still in place. Critics link it to slow housebuilding and high land prices.

context: Final abolition of the Poor Law.
did: Created means-tested national assistance as a safety net and gave councils a duty to provide residential accommodation for people needing care.
effects: The origin of the split between free NHS care and means-tested council social care, which remains a central unresolved problem.

context: The Redcliffe-Maud commission on local government.
did: Created the two-tier system of counties and districts in England and Wales from 1974.
effects: Much of today's English local government map. Unitary reorganisations have been reshaping it ever since.

did: Gave council tenants the Right to Buy their homes at large discounts.
effects: Roughly 2 million homes sold in England, with receipts not fully reinvested in new social housing. Social housing stock fell and temporary accommodation costs for councils later rose.

context: Conflict between central government and the metropolitan councils.
did: Abolished the Greater London Council and the six metropolitan county councils in 1986.
effects: London had no city-wide government until the GLA in 2000; the metropolitan areas regained strategic bodies only with combined authorities after 2011.

context: Concern over standards and the power of local education authorities.
did: Introduced the national curriculum, national testing, delegated budgets to schools and allowed schools to opt out of council control.
effects: The template for league tables, Ofsted inspection (from 1992) and later academies.

did: Introduced the community charge (poll tax), a flat per-adult charge, and nationalised business rates.
effects: Mass non-payment and the 1990 riots. It was replaced by council tax within three years, but the national business rates system remains.

did: Sold the ten English and Welsh water and sewerage authorities and created Ofwat and the National Rivers Authority.
effects: Investment rose but so did debt and dividends. Sewage spills and the absence of new reservoirs since the early 1990s led to the Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 and a review of regulation.

t: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990
did: Created the NHS internal market (purchasers and providers, NHS trusts) and moved responsibility for community care to councils.
effects: The purchaser/provider split survived in various forms until the Health and Care Act 2022 moved back towards collaboration.

did: Created council tax, levied on homes in bands A to H.
effects: England's bands still rest on 1991 values, so the tax is regressive relative to current property values. Councils rely on it for an increasing share of their income.

did: Split the railway into track (Railtrack) and train operating franchises, with rolling stock leasing companies and a regulator.
effects: Passenger numbers roughly doubled to 2019, but costs rose. Railtrack failed in 2001 and was replaced by Network Rail, and franchising is being ended by the 2024 public ownership Act.

context: Equalising pension ages, and the Maxwell scandal.
did: Equalised the state pension age for women at 65 (phased from 2010) and strengthened occupational pension regulation.
effects: The way the change was communicated was later found to be maladministration by the Parliamentary Ombudsman (the WASPI campaign).

context: Taking interest rates out of politics.
did: Gave the Bank of England operational independence over monetary policy through the Monetary Policy Committee.
effects: The basis of today's monetary regime. It is why the simulator assumes monetary policy offsets fiscal demand effects over time.

did: Created a statutory minimum wage set on the advice of the Low Pay Commission.
effects: Large real rises in pay for the lowest paid with little measured job loss; since 2016 the higher 'National Living Wage' rate has applied.

context: Bringing the European Convention on Human Rights into domestic law.
did: Allowed Convention rights to be enforced in UK courts and required public bodies to act compatibly.
effects: Shapes immigration, policing and public service decisions. Article 1 of Protocol 1 (property) constrains compulsory acquisition, as in the model lab.

did: Created the Scottish Parliament and Government with power over devolved matters, funded by the block grant.
effects: Devolved health, education and much else, so many English figures in this app do not cover Scotland. The Barnett formula sets its funding.

did: Created the Mayor of London and the London Assembly, with Transport for London.
effects: The model for elected metro mayors in other English city regions.

did: Created a right of access to information held by public authorities.
effects: Much of the data behind this app exists because of it. Its exemptions are why some major project ratings are withheld.

context: Making work pay and reducing child poverty.
did: Created child tax credit and working tax credit, run by HMRC.
effects: Child poverty fell sharply in the 2000s; overpayments were a long-running problem. Being replaced by Universal Credit.

context: Slow consents for big infrastructure such as Heathrow Terminal 5.
did: Created development consent orders for nationally significant infrastructure projects, decided by ministers after examination.
effects: Consent times have lengthened since the early 2010s. The Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 reformed the regime again.

context: The first national legally binding emissions target.
did: Set a legally binding emissions target (80% by 2050, raised to net zero in 2019), five-yearly carbon budgets and the Climate Change Committee.
effects: UK territorial emissions roughly halved from 1990 by the early 2020s, mostly by removing coal from electricity generation.

did: Let any maintained school convert to an academy funded directly by the DfE, and allowed free schools.
effects: Most secondary schools and over 40% of primaries are now academies, often in multi-academy trusts, as shown in the education section.

context: Putting the civil service on a statutory footing.
did: Gave the civil service a statutory basis, with the core values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and appointment on merit.
effects: The legal frame for any civil service reorganisation tested in the model lab.

did: Brought nine protected characteristics into one Act and created the public sector equality duty.
effects: Every policy in the drafting workspace should be checked against the public sector equality duty.

t: Budget Responsibility and National Audit Act 2011
did: Put the Office for Budget Responsibility on a statutory footing and required a Charter for Budget Responsibility setting the fiscal rules.
effects: OBR forecasts are the baseline used by this app's simulator.

did: Gave councils a general power of competence and required referendums for council tax rises above a set limit.
effects: The power of competence enabled commercial investments that later contributed to failures such as Thurrock and Woking. The referendum limit caps council tax rises.

context: Simplifying means-tested benefits and cutting spending.
did: Created Universal Credit, Personal Independence Payment and the benefit cap.
effects: Universal Credit rollout ran years late. Spending on health and disability benefits has since grown fastest, as the social security section shows.

did: Abolished primary care trusts and strategic health authorities, created clinical commissioning groups and NHS England, and extended competition.
effects: Widely judged disruptive. It was largely reversed by the Health and Care Act 2022.

context: The Dilnot commission on social care funding.
did: Set out councils' duties for adult social care and legislated for a cap on lifetime care costs.
effects: The cap has been repeatedly deferred and never introduced. Adult social care is the largest pressure on council budgets.

did: Replaced SEN statements with education, health and care (EHC) plans running from 0 to 25, with legal entitlements.
effects: EHC plans have more than doubled. The high-needs (DSG) deficits shown in the councils section stem from this demand, and they are a lever in the simulator.

did: Introduced the single-tier new state pension from April 2016 and brought forward the rise in pension age to 67.
effects: Together with the triple lock, it makes the state pension the largest single benefit.

t: Cities and Local Government Devolution Act 2016
did: Allowed combined authorities to have directly elected mayors and to take on transferred functions.
effects: Created metro mayors such as Greater Manchester and the West Midlands. Deeper devolution is now set out in the English Devolution bill.

t: High Speed Rail (London - West Midlands) Act 2017
context: Capacity on the West Coast Main Line.
did: Authorised construction of HS2 Phase 1 from London to Birmingham.
effects: Costs have risen far beyond the original budget and the northern legs were cancelled in 2023. HS2 is in the major projects section.

did: Placed new duties on English councils to prevent and relieve homelessness for all eligible applicants.
effects: More people are helped earlier, but temporary accommodation numbers and costs have reached record levels.

did: Repealed the European Communities Act 1972 and converted EU law into 'retained' domestic law.
effects: Created a large body of law that ministers can amend by regulations. Net EU transfers fell to near zero, as the spending tables show.

did: Gave emergency powers over health services, registration of deaths, statutory sick pay and more.
effects: Pandemic spending pushed debt above 95% of GDP. Most of the Act's powers have since expired.

did: Requires notification of acquisitions in 17 sensitive sectors and lets ministers block or impose conditions on deals.
effects: It limits resale of seized assets abroad in the model lab's economic cycle.

did: Abolished clinical commissioning groups and created 42 integrated care boards with integrated care partnerships, from 1 July 2022.
effects: Integrated care boards are on the NHS map. Further mergers of the boards and the abolition of NHS England were announced in 2025.

did: Created the Building Safety Regulator and a new regime for higher-risk buildings, and protected leaseholders from some remediation costs.
effects: Remediation of unsafe cladding is still running years later, and building control gateways have slowed some housebuilding.

did: Set principles that public subsidies to firms must meet.
effects: Applies to any below-market hand-over of assets to a national champion in the model lab.

did: Created a single procurement regime with a central platform, more flexible procedures and a debarment list, in force from February 2025.
effects: Changes the contract notices shown in the contracts section.

did: Set statutory levelling-up missions, reformed plan-making and created a framework for devolution deals.
effects: Parts were superseded by the 2024 government's planning reforms.

did: Lets passenger services transfer to public ownership as each contract expires.
effects: Operators are moving into public ownership ahead of Great British Railways.

context: The 2022 mini-budget, which had no OBR forecast.
did: Requires an OBR assessment of any fiscally significant measure (above 1% of GDP).
effects: The 'fiscal lock'. Large scenarios in the simulator would trigger it.

context: Sewage spills and water company finances.
did: Strengthened Ofwat's powers on bonuses and governance and toughened penalties for pollution.
effects: Part of a wider overhaul of water regulation following the Cunliffe review.

context: The target of 1.5 million homes and faster infrastructure consents.
did: Reformed infrastructure consents, introduced a nature restoration levy and development corporations, and changed compulsory purchase.
effects: Too early to measure. Its effect on housebuilding is a lever to test in the simulator.

did: Expanded day-one rights, curbed zero-hours contracts and fire-and-rehire, and reformed trade union law.
effects: Phased in from 2026. The OBR and the government's impact assessment differ on its employment effects.
